extracted.intended_audience: aspiring newspaper reporters / journalism students / newsroom novices
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for entry-level newspaper reporters on how to gather, write, and present copy that meets newsroom standards (accuracy, objectivity, neatness, and production constraints). Emphasizes fact-checking, clean manuscript practices, and cooperation with production departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision (exactness of fact and statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In getting news, the reporter faces a constant demand for exactness, both of fact and of statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hedging and circumlocution (example: don't write 'approximately dozen years' — give the exact number). Re-check numerical and factual details (e.g., exact temperature: 84 or 85 at 7 o'clock). Editors will demand exact figures and precise wording; imprecision will be called out and corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / avoid editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell what people did and said, and let the readers decide whether it was good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert subjective judgments into news copy (e.g., writing 'another far-fetched speech' is improper). Report actions and quotes; leave evaluation to readers or editorial pages. The city editor explicitly instructs reporters to report causes 'right' rather than offering personal opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / no excuse for mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: There shouldn't be mistakes; newspapers 'wince for every one of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes have immediate consequences (phone calls, letters); time pressure is not an excuse. Even obvious errors (typos, wrong headlines) lead to stopping a press run and delaying an edition. Aim to eliminate errors because the production process magnifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking / verify names, places, and details
rubrics_metrics.description: Find out once and for all, and find out right (e.g., correct railroad crossing, correct middle initials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check proper names, addresses, locations, and identifying details before submitting copy. The city editor will return copy to be corrected if facts conflict; verification prevents reader complaints and preserves credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the house style (style sheet and newsroom preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every office gives its newcomers a how-to-do-it manual explaining its preferences and prohibitions; the style sheet inevitably opens, ends, and is punctuated with exhortations; 'Accuracy Always.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and adhere to the paper's style sheet and conventions (preferred spellings, headline conventions, punctuation, preferred formats). House style governs what is wanted on Monday vs Wednesday and affects editing decisions and promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean copy (neatness and legibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean copy suggests thoroughness and care; dirty copy bespeaks sloven and dingy work and hence carelessness as to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit typed, readable, and neatly corrected copy. Excessive pencil scrawls, insertions between lines, and muddled corrections make editing difficult and invite decimation of the story. Recopy if there are many amendments. Clean copy moves through the desk faster and improves assignment prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typing accuracy (accuracy before speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether he uses the touch or the hunt-and-peck system, a reporter should perfect his typing as rapidly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize accuracy; speed will follow. Poor typing produces dirty copy. Establish the habit of accurate typing early to avoid persistent messy copy that harms professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear conventions for handwritten corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: When he makes a longhand correction, the reporter carefully distinguishes between letters confusingly alike (overscore or underscore similar letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, consistent correction marks: overscore o, m, n and underscore a, w, u; cut and paste paragraphs to change sequence instead of messy arrows. Neat correction practices reduce errors in transcription and recomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work to production/format constraints (write to fit composing needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: At 9 in the morning the editors send news in 500-word stories; at 1 in the afternoon the editors may slice news into 100-word or 50-word fragments... short section fits better into the composing room's necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that copy will be adjusted for typesetting and page makeup; write with flexible lengths and clear modular paragraphs so editors can trim without destroying meaning. Understand that edition/page limits (e.g., Saturday edition) require severe compression sometimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation and teamwork across departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each department is as independent as the weather, yet the newspaper cannot be issued unless each department cooperates constantly and thoroughly with the other divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the roles and constraints of business, advertising, editorial, mechanical production, and circulation. Provide copy and materials that help composing, engraving, and press run smoothly; anticipate production needs (wordage, formatting) to avoid waste and delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial integrity tied to financial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The American newspaper is founded upon mechanical competency, commercial sagacity, and editorial integrity. There can be no editorial integrity without financial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the relationship between editorial freedom and the paper's financial footing. In markets where advertising/circulation revenue is weak, editorial content may be compromised; reporters should value honesty and intelligence in reporting made possible by independent finances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean copy as indicator of professionalism and promotability
rubrics_metrics.description: The city editor looks closely at the cleanness or mossiness of reporters' copy; clean copy is an indication of its writer's mental attitude and trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently submitting clean copy improves chances for better assignments and promotion; sloppy copy results in poor assignments and returns for rewriting. The probationary period shortens for those who are 'clean' writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect inspection and proofreading by copy desk and composing room
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy desk crew inspect all the news; the composing room examines every line to see that it is free from error; obvious mistakes are corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume multiple layers of editorial and production proofreading. Make it easy for copy editors and compositors by reducing errors, following correction conventions, and checking your work before submission to minimize rework and press delays.
